''Structure generated from the source by <code>reference.py</code>; the explanations come from <code>reference_notes.py</code>. Do not edit this file -- edit those and re-run.''

<code>iw</code> is a small Python library that mirrors the game engine's world-definition JSON as typed dataclasses, and serializes them to and from that JSON. Use it to build world definitions programmatically, or to read and round-trip existing ones. Its only dependency is PyYAML, which Pyodide ships, so it runs in a browser unchanged — and it is standalone in the sense that matters here: it does '''not''' require [[plot]].

This page is '''every object in <code>iw</code>, every attribute on it, and every enum member''' — what each one is, what it is for, and how it is used. The structure is read out of the dataclasses themselves, so it cannot fall behind the library; the explanations sit beside it rather than in a separate document.

A field you never set gets the default shown, and a default the engine is happy with — so in practice you name only the handful you care about.

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
import iw
</syntaxhighlight>

A world is an <code>iw.World</code>. It holds content (characters, NPCs, instruction blocks, lorebook entries, tracked items, image/style settings) plus an '''event system''' (<code>triggerEvents</code>) that drives dynamic behaviour. You assemble a <code>World</code> from the dataclasses below and call <code>.to_json()</code> to get the engine's JSON; or parse engine JSON back with <code>World.from_json()</code>.

=== <code>InitialTrackedItemValue</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! attribute !! type !! default !! what it's for
|-
| <code>id</code> || <code>str</code> || <code>required</code> || The id of the tracked item this value is for.
|-
| <code>name</code> || <code>str</code> || <code>required</code> || That item's name, repeated.
|-
| <code>initialPCValue</code> || `str \ || list[str]` || <code>''</code> || This character's starting value — or a list of options to choose between.
|-
| <code>visibility</code> || <code>TrackedItemVisibility</code> || <code>TrackedItemVisibility.AI_ONLY</code> || Who can see it, for this character.
|-
| <code>initialValueBasedOnPC</code> || <code>TrackedItemInitialValueSource</code> || <code>TrackedItemInitialValueSource.CHARACTER</code> || Mirrors the item's own mode; an entry declaring anything but <code>CHARACTER</code> is dropped on import.
|-
| <code>initialPCValueChoicesScript</code> || <code>Optional[str]</code> || <code>None</code> || A <code>$</code>-script yielding this character's options.

One of these exists per character for each <code>CHARACTER</code>-mode tracked item — they are not free-form overrides you attach at will. See Initial values.

<code>item.variable_name</code> is the item's handle — its <code>variableName</code> if one is set, otherwise the name lowercased with spaces → underscores. A '''renamed item keeps its original handle''', so it is this, not the visible <code>name</code>, that a <code>$</code>-script or a substitution refers to. <code>item.as_substitution()</code> wraps it as <code>&lt;&lt;…&gt;&gt;</code> for embedding in trigger and instruction text.

Where an item's starting value comes from is a whole topic of its own — see Initial values below.

The engine fills in extra keys on some payloads that you do not have to write: <code>path</code>, <code>updateMode</code>, <code>listExpression</code> and <code>targetExpression</code> on <code>SET_TRACKED_ITEM_VALUE</code>, <code>path</code>/<code>updateMode</code> on <code>PRESENT_CHOICE</code> and <code>REQUEST_INPUT</code>, and <code>alreadyFired</code> on a victory/defeat condition.

=== <code>TriggerCondition</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! attribute !! type !! default !! what it's for
|-
| <code>data</code> || <code>Any</code> || <code>required</code> || The payload. Its shape depends on <code>type</code> — see the condition table.
|-
| <code>id</code> || <code>str</code> || <code>auto</code> || Its own id.
|-
| <code>type</code> || <code>Optional[ConditionType]</code> || <code>None</code> || Which kind of condition. Absent on a logic group.
|-
| <code>category</code> || <code>Optional[str]</code> || <code>None</code> || <code>"condition"</code> for a leaf, <code>"logic"</code> for a group.
|-
| <code>trackedItemID</code> || <code>Optional[str]</code> || <code>None</code> || The item read, repeated outside <code>data</code> — both copies must agree.
|-
| <code>inequality</code> || <code>Optional[Inequality]</code> || <code>None</code> || The comparison, written here as well as in <code>data</code>, and only when it is not the default.
|-
| <code>operator</code> || <code>Optional[LogicOperator]</code> || <code>None</code> || <code>AND</code> / <code>OR</code>, on a logic group.
|}

Set either a <code>type</code> (a leaf condition) or <code>category="logic"</code> with an <code>operator</code> (a group combining sub-conditions). A group's <code>data</code> holds <code>TriggerCondition</code>s whether you built the group or parsed one — a parsed group's raw sub-dicts are built out on construction — and the owning <code>TriggerEvent</code> needs <code>advancedLogic=True</code>. Every leaf condition carries <code>category="condition"</code>; the helpers set it for you.

* <code>world.to_dict()</code> / <code>world.to_json()</code> — emit the engine JSON. Optional fields are omitted while still at their default, and <code>positionInList</code> is stamped onto tracked items and NPCs.
* <code>iw.World.from_dict(data)</code> / <code>iw.World.from_json(s)</code> — parse engine JSON back into dataclasses. Parsing is '''strict''': an unknown field raises <code>NotImplementedError</code>, so the dataclasses stay a faithful mirror of the schema.
* <code>world.validate()</code> — raise <code>ValueError</code> listing everything that doesn't hang together. '''<code>to_json()</code> calls this for you''', so a broken world raises instead of becoming a file.
* <code>world.summary()</code> — a readable account of what is in the world. Print it before and after a change.

The dangling-reference case is worth dwelling on, because it is the one that bites. Triggers name their tracked items, blocks and characters '''by id'''. If a trigger holds an id nothing answers to any more, the engine loads the world perfectly happily — and then that trigger simply never fires. Nothing tells you. You find it by playing. So the library refuses to write that file at all.

== The enums ==

Every one is a <code>StrEnum</code>, so a member ''is'' the string the engine reads — you can pass the member or its value and the JSON comes out the same. Prefer the member: a typo in a member name is an <code>AttributeError</code>, and a typo in a string is a world that loads and quietly does nothing.

The examples below all run, and refer to these:

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
mood    = iw.TrackedItem(name="Mood", initialValue="calm")
crew    = iw.TrackedItem(name="Crew", dataType=iw.TrackedItemDataType.NUMBER, initialValue="4")
roster  = iw.TrackedItem(name="Roster", dataType=iw.TrackedItemDataType.YAML)
rules   = iw.InstructionBlock(name="Rules", content="Be terse.")
dragons = iw.LoreBookEntry(name="Dragons", content="They sleep.", keywords=["dragon"])
ambush  = iw.TriggerEvent(name="Ambush")
storm   = iw.TriggerEvent(name="Storm")
hero    = iw.PossibleCharacter(name="Hero")
ferryman = iw.NPC(name="The Ferryman", detail="A silent boatman.")
harbourmaster = iw.NPC(name="The Harbourmaster", detail="Keeper of the tide tables.")
</syntaxhighlight>

=== <code>TrackedItemDataType</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>TEXT</code> || <code>text</code> || A plain string. The default. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Mood", dataType=iw.TrackedItemDataType.TEXT, initialValue="calm")</code>
|-
| <code>NUMBER</code> || <code>number</code> || A number, still carried as a string. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Crew", dataType=iw.TrackedItemDataType.NUMBER, initialValue="4")</code>
|-
| <code>XML</code> || <code>xml</code> || Structured data as XML. Semi-deprecated — prefer <code>YAML</code>. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Party", dataType=iw.TrackedItemDataType.XML)</code>
|-
| <code>YAML</code> || <code>yaml</code> || Structured data as a YAML document: nested maps and lists, reachable from <code>$</code>-scripts. The going-forward type. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Roster", dataType=iw.TrackedItemDataType.YAML, initialValue="members:\n  - name: Ivo")</code>
|}

=== <code>TrackedItemVisibility</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>EVERYONE</code> || <code>everyone</code> || Shown to the player and given to the AI. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Mood", visibility=iw.TrackedItemVisibility.EVERYONE)</code>
|-
| <code>AI_ONLY</code> || <code>ai_only</code> || Given to the AI, never shown to the player. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Suspicion", visibility=iw.TrackedItemVisibility.AI_ONLY)</code>
|-
| <code>PLAYER_ONLY</code> || <code>player_only</code> || Shown to the player, withheld from the AI. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Notes", visibility=iw.TrackedItemVisibility.PLAYER_ONLY)</code>
|-
| <code>HIDDEN</code> || <code>hidden</code> || Hidden in normal play; visible in storyteller mode. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Stage", visibility=iw.TrackedItemVisibility.HIDDEN)</code>
|-
| <code>HIDDEN_BORING</code> || <code>hidden_boring</code> || Hidden in normal play; visible only in debug mode. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Turn counter", visibility=iw.TrackedItemVisibility.HIDDEN_BORING)</code>
|}

<code>HIDDEN</code> and <code>HIDDEN_BORING</code> both hide an item from the player in normal play; the difference is ''where'' it still shows. <code>HIDDEN</code> is visible in '''storyteller mode''', <code>HIDDEN_BORING</code> only in '''debug mode'''. Reach for <code>HIDDEN_BORING</code> for bookkeeping the storyteller never needs to see.

=== <code>TrackedItemInitialValueSource</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>SAME</code> || <code>same</code> || Every playthrough starts from the item's own <code>initialValue</code>. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Mood", initialValueBasedOnPC=iw.TrackedItemInitialValueSource.SAME, initialValue="calm")</code>
|-
| <code>CHARACTER</code> || <code>character</code> || The value depends on which character is chosen, and lives on each character. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Homeland", initialValueBasedOnPC=iw.TrackedItemInitialValueSource.CHARACTER)</code>
|-
| <code>PLAYER</code> || <code>player</code> || The player enters it; <code>initialValue</code> is the default they edit. || <code>iw.TrackedItem(name="Callsign", initialValueBasedOnPC=iw.TrackedItemInitialValueSource.PLAYER, initialValue="Nomad")</code>
|}

Which mode an item is in decides ''where its starting value lives'' — see Initial values below.

=== <code>TrackedItemAction</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>SET</code> || <code>set</code> || Overwrite the value. || <code>set_tracked_item(mood, "uneasy")</code>
|-
| <code>ADD</code> || <code>add</code> || Add to it. || <code>set_tracked_item(crew, "1", action=iw.TrackedItemAction.ADD)</code>
|-
| <code>SUBTRACT</code> || <code>subtract</code> || Take away from it. || <code>set_tracked_item(crew, "1", action=iw.TrackedItemAction.SUBTRACT)</code>
|-
| <code>REPLACE</code> || <code>replace</code> || Find <code>newValue</code> and swap in <code>replaceWith</code> — here the value you pass is the needle, not the result. || <code>set_tracked_item(mood, "calm", action=iw.TrackedItemAction.REPLACE)</code>
|}

=== <code>NPCAction</code> ===

What <code>CHANGE_OTHER_CHARACTERS</code> does to the NPC it names. Separate from <code>TrackedItemAction</code> despite both living in an effect's <code>data["action"]</code>: the two sets never overlap.

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>ADD</code> || <code>add</code> || Bring a new NPC into the world mid-game. The only action with nothing to match on, so <code>data["character"]</code> is <code>None</code>; the NPC in <code>data["npc"]</code> is the one being created. It carries no <code>positionInList</code> either — the engine appends it and assigns the position, where <code>MODIFY</code> and <code>DELETE</code> name an NPC that already has one. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_OTHER_CHARACTERS, data={"character": None, "action": iw.NPCAction.ADD, "npc": {"id": harbourmaster.id, "name": harbourmaster.name, "detail": harbourmaster.detail}})</code>
|-
| <code>MODIFY</code> || <code>modify</code> || Replace the NPC with the one in <code>data["npc"]</code>, matched by <code>data["character"]</code>. The whole NPC is written, not the changed fields, so send it as it should end up. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_OTHER_CHARACTERS, data={"character": ferryman.name, "action": iw.NPCAction.MODIFY, "npc": {"id": ferryman.id, "name": ferryman.name, "detail": "He speaks now."}})</code>
|-
| <code>DELETE</code> || <code>delete</code> || Remove the NPC from the world. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_OTHER_CHARACTERS, data={"character": ferryman.name, "action": iw.NPCAction.DELETE, "npc": {"id": ferryman.id, "name": ferryman.name}})</code>
|}

=== <code>Inequality</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>IS_EXACTLY</code> || <code>is_exactly</code> || Equal. The default, and the one the engine does not write down. || <code>tracked_item_is(mood, "uneasy")</code>
|-
| <code>AT_LEAST</code> || <code>at_least</code> || Greater than or equal. || <code>tracked_item_is(crew, "2", inequality=iw.Inequality.AT_LEAST)</code>
|-
| <code>AT_MOST</code> || <code>at_most</code> || Less than or equal. || <code>tracked_item_is(crew, "2", inequality=iw.Inequality.AT_MOST)</code>
|-
| <code>NOT_EQUAL</code> || <code>not_equal</code> || Different. || <code>tracked_item_is(mood, "calm", inequality=iw.Inequality.NOT_EQUAL)</code>
|}

=== <code>EffectType</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>SHOW_MESSAGE</code> || <code>effectShowMessage</code> || Shows the player a message, outside the narration. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.SHOW_MESSAGE, data="The bridge collapses behind you.")</code>
|-
| <code>GIVE_INFO</code> || <code>effectGiveInfo</code> || Tells the AI something out of band, without narrating it. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.GIVE_INFO, data="The captain is lying about the cargo.")</code>
|-
| <code>TELL_AI</code> || <code>effectTellAIWhatToDo</code> || Instructs the AI on what to do next. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.TELL_AI, data="Raise the tension. End the scene on a threat.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_MAIN_INSTRUCTIONS</code> || <code>effectChangeMainInstructions</code> || Rewrites the main instructions. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_MAIN_INSTRUCTIONS, data="I am now the hunted, not the hunter.")</code>
|-
| <code>MODIFY_INSTRUCTION_BLOCK</code> || <code>effectModifyInstructionBlock</code> || Rewrites a block's text. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.MODIFY_INSTRUCTION_BLOCK, data={"id": rules.id, "content": "Be terse. Never explain the magic."})</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_AUTHOR_STYLE</code> || <code>effectChangeAuthorStyle</code> || Rewrites the author-style voice. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_AUTHOR_STYLE, data="Terse, clipped, hard-boiled.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_DESCRIPTION_INSTRUCTIONS</code> || <code>effectChangeDescriptionInstructions</code> || Rewrites the description-request instructions. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_DESCRIPTION_INSTRUCTIONS, data="Describe each scene in two sentences, no more.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_OBJECTIVE</code> || <code>effectChangeObjective</code> || Rewrites the on-screen goal. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_OBJECTIVE, data="Escape the city before dawn.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_BACKGROUND</code> || <code>effectChangeBackground</code> || Rewrites the background. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_BACKGROUND, data="A drowned city, ruled by salvage crews.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_FIRST_ACTION</code> || <code>effectChangeFirstAction</code> || Rewrites <code>firstInput</code>, before the first turn. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_FIRST_ACTION, data="I wake to alarms.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_VICTORY_CONDITION</code> || <code>effectChangeVictoryCondition</code> || Replaces the victory condition. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_VICTORY_CONDITION, data={"condition": "I reach the lighthouse", "text": "You made it."})</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_DEFEAT_CONDITION</code> || <code>effectChangeDefeatCondition</code> || Replaces the defeat condition. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_DEFEAT_CONDITION, data={"condition": "the crew all die", "text": "Nobody came home."})</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_PC_NAME</code> || <code>effectChangePCName</code> || Renames the playing character. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_PC_NAME, data="The Stranger")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_PC_DESCRIPTION</code> || <code>effectChangePCDescription</code> || Rewrites the playing character's description. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_PC_DESCRIPTION, data="Scarred, quiet, unwilling to explain the coat.")</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_PC_SKILL</code> || <code>effectChangePCSkill</code> || Raises (<code>increase=True</code>) or lowers a skill by <code>amount</code>, clamped at <code>minmax</code>. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_PC_SKILL, data={"name": "Nerve", "amount": 1, "minmax": 5, "increase": True})</code>
|-
| <code>CHANGE_OTHER_CHARACTERS</code> || <code>effectChangeOtherCharacters</code> || Adds, rewrites or removes an NPC. <code>data</code> is <code>{character, action, npc}</code> — <code>character</code> names the one to act on (<code>None</code> when adding, as there is nothing to match yet), <code>action</code> is an <code>NPCAction</code>, and <code>npc</code> is the whole NPC as it should end up. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.CHANGE_OTHER_CHARACTERS, data={"character": ferryman.name, "action": iw.NPCAction.MODIFY, "npc": {"id": ferryman.id, "name": ferryman.name, "detail": "He speaks now."}})</code>
|-
| <code>SET_TRACKED_ITEM_VALUE</code> || <code>effectSetTrackedItemValue</code> || Writes a tracked item. <code>data</code> is <code>{action, newValue, replaceWith, trackedItemID}</code>; the <code>action</code> decides how — see <code>TrackedItemAction</code>. || <code>set_tracked_item(mood, "uneasy")</code>
|-
| <code>RUN_SCRIPT</code> || <code>effectRunScript</code> || Runs a <code>$</code>-script block. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.RUN_SCRIPT, data="for each $m in $roster.party\n  $m.hp += 5")</code>
|-
| <code>FIRE_RANDOM_TRIGGER</code> || <code>effectFireRandomTrigger</code> || Fires one of the listed triggers at random. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.FIRE_RANDOM_TRIGGER, data=[ambush.id, storm.id])</code>
|-
| <code>MODIFY_KEYWORD_BLOCK</code> || <code>effectModifyKeywordBlock</code> || The same for a lorebook entry, and rewrites its keywords too. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.MODIFY_KEYWORD_BLOCK, data={"id": dragons.id, "content": "They are awake now.", "keywords": ["dragon", "wyrm"]})</code>
|-
| <code>ENDS_GAME</code> || <code>effectEndsGame</code> || Ends the game. <code>data</code> is the <code>can_continue</code> value — <code>False</code> is a hard ending. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.ENDS_GAME, data=False)</code>
|-
| <code>MODIFY_TRACKED_ITEM_DETAILS</code> || <code>effectModifyTrackedItemDetails</code> || Changes an item's own name / description / visibility / update instructions. Each field you change needs its <code>override*</code> flag set alongside it. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.MODIFY_TRACKED_ITEM_DETAILS, data={"trackedItemID": mood.id, "overrideName": True, "name": "Temper"})</code>
|-
| <code>PRESENT_CHOICE</code> || <code>effectPresentChoice</code> || Offers the player a choice; the picked value(s) land in the target item. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.PRESENT_CHOICE, data={"message": "Which way?", "choices": "Left\nRight", "selectionMode": "single", "valueDelimiter": "newline", "minSelections": 1, "maxSelections": 1, "targetTrackedItemId": mood.id})</code>
|-
| <code>REQUEST_INPUT</code> || <code>effectRequestInput</code> || Prompts the player for text; the reply lands in the target item. || <code>iw.TriggerEffect(type=iw.EffectType.REQUEST_INPUT, data={"inputMode": "single", "requestText": "Name yourself.", "requiresInput": True, "targetTrackedItemId": mood.id})</code>
|}

<code>minSelections</code>/<code>maxSelections</code> come back as ints from some triggers and strings from others — read both.

=== <code>ConditionType</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>ON_TURN</code> || <code>triggerOnTurn</code> || Fires on turn '''≥ N''', not exactly N. <code>data=1</code> is the "every turn" idiom. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(type=iw.ConditionType.ON_TURN, category="condition", data=1)</code>
|-
| <code>ON_EVENT</code> || <code>triggerOnEvent</code> || Fires when the AI judges the described situation to have happened. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(type=iw.ConditionType.ON_EVENT, category="condition", data="the crew mutinies")</code>
|-
| <code>ON_CHARACTER</code> || <code>triggerOnCharacter</code> || Gates on who the player picked. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(type=iw.ConditionType.ON_CHARACTER, category="condition", data=[hero.characterId])</code>
|-
| <code>ON_TRACKED_ITEM</code> || <code>triggerOnTrackedItem</code> || Reads a tracked item. <code>data</code> is <code>{inequality, requiredValue, trackedItemID, textComparison}</code>. <code>textComparison</code> is '''required''' (<code>"contains"</code> / <code>"does_not_contain"</code>) — a condition without it is dropped on import. Text items have ''no'' exact match, only contains. <code>tracked_item_is</code> fills it in for you. || <code>tracked_item_is(mood, "uneasy")</code>
|-
| <code>ON_RANDOM_CHANCE</code> || <code>triggerOnRandomChance</code> || Fires that percent of the time. The percentage is a '''string'''. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(type=iw.ConditionType.ON_RANDOM_CHANCE, category="condition", data="37")</code>
|-
| <code>ON_PAW_SCRIPT</code> || <code>triggerOnPawScript</code> || Fires when a <code>$</code>-expression is true. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(type=iw.ConditionType.ON_PAW_SCRIPT, category="condition", data="$roster.party.count()&gt;0")</code>
|-
| <code>PREREQS</code> || <code>triggerPrereqs</code> || Fires only once the listed triggers have. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(type=iw.ConditionType.PREREQS, category="condition", data=[ambush.id])</code>
|}

Every leaf condition carries <code>category="condition"</code>; the helpers set it for you. A '''logic group''' is a condition with no <code>type</code> at all — <code>category="logic"</code> and an <code>operator</code> — whose <code>data</code> is a list of sub-conditions. It nests arbitrarily, and its <code>TriggerEvent</code> needs <code>advancedLogic=True</code>:

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
iw.TriggerCondition(category="logic", operator=iw.LogicOperator.OR, data=[
    tracked_item_is(mood, "uneasy"),
    tracked_item_is(crew, "2", inequality=iw.Inequality.AT_MOST),
])
</syntaxhighlight>

=== <code>LogicOperator</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! member !! value in the JSON !! what it does !! example
|-
| <code>AND</code> || <code>and</code> || Every sub-condition must hold. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(category="logic", operator=iw.LogicOperator.AND, data=[tracked_item_is(mood, "uneasy"), tracked_item_is(crew, "2", inequality=iw.Inequality.AT_MOST)])</code>
|-
| <code>OR</code> || <code>or</code> || Any sub-condition may hold. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(category="logic", operator=iw.LogicOperator.OR, data=[tracked_item_is(mood, "uneasy"), tracked_item_is(mood, "afraid")])</code>
|-
| <code>NONE_OF</code> || <code>none_of</code> || No sub-condition may hold — the negation the other two cannot express. Wrapping a single condition in it is how you say ''unless''. || <code>iw.TriggerCondition(category="logic", operator=iw.LogicOperator.NONE_OF, data=[tracked_item_is(mood, "calm")])</code>
|}

== The functions ==

=== <code>reset_ids(seed: int = 0) -&gt; None</code> ===

Reset the shared ID generator. Ids are drawn from one seeded sequence, so a world's ids depend on everything generated before it in the same process. Call this before building a world to make its output reproducible no matter what else was built first (the build script does).

== Initial values: <code>same</code> / <code>character</code> / <code>player</code> ==

A tracked item's <code>initialValueBasedOnPC</code> picks where its starting value comes from. The three modes put that value in three ''different places'', which is the part worth knowing:

{| class="wikitable"
! mode !! the UI's wording !! where the value lives
|-
| <code>SAME</code> || initial value is always the same || the item's own <code>initialValue</code>
|-
| <code>CHARACTER</code> || depends on which character the player chooses || one entry per character under <code>possibleCharacters[].initialTrackedItemValues</code>; the item's own <code>initialValue</code> stays empty
|-
| <code>PLAYER</code> || can be entered by the player || the item's own <code>initialValue</code>, acting as the default the player edits
|}

Both <code>PLAYER</code> and <code>CHARACTER</code> can offer the player a '''list to choose from''' instead of free text — given either literally or as a <code>$</code>-script yielding the options — but each mode carries it on a different object, and the near-identical field names are easy to mix up:

{| class="wikitable"
!  !! literal choices !! script yielding choices !! the value itself
|-
| <code>PLAYER</code> — on the '''item''' || <code>initialValueChoices</code> || <code>initialValueChoicesScript</code> || <code>initialValue</code> (the default selection)
|-
| <code>CHARACTER</code> — on the '''per-character entry''' || <code>initialPCValue</code> ''as a list'' || <code>initialPCValueChoicesScript</code> || <code>initialPCValue</code>
|}

Per-character entries are not free-form overrides you attach at will: a character carries '''one entry per <code>CHARACTER</code>-mode item''', and the entry's own <code>initialValueBasedOnPC</code> mirrors the item's. An entry declaring any other mode has no item it can belong to and is dropped on import.

== Scripting & structured data ==

The engine has a <code>$</code>-expression scripting language and structured (YAML) tracked items. <code>iw</code> models the enum values and passes the script text through verbatim; the language itself is the engine's. <code>TrackedItemDataType.YAML</code> holds the document, <code>ConditionType.ON_PAW_SCRIPT</code> reads an expression, and <code>EffectType.RUN_SCRIPT</code> runs a block. The <code>TrackedItem</code> fields the feature needs — <code>variableName</code>, <code>enforceFormat</code>, <code>formatSchema</code>, <code>formatExample</code>, <code>driftAcknowledgedForName</code>, and the two <code>initialValueChoices*</code> fields — all default to <code>None</code> and strip from output unless set, so worlds predating the feature serialise unchanged.

== IDs & helpers ==

Objects that need an id get one from a shared, deterministic <code>IDGenerator</code>, and '''nothing in this repo ever writes one by hand'''. <code>World.from_dict</code> re-seeds it from the parsed data so ids created afterwards cannot collide with the parsed world's. <code>iw.reset_ids()</code> makes a build reproducible regardless of what was built before it (the build script calls it).

<code>set_tracked_item(item, value, action=SET)</code> and <code>tracked_item_is(item, value, inequality=IS_EXACTLY)</code> build the effect that writes a tracked item and the condition that reads one. '''Use them.''' The engine's payload for both carries the item's id ''twice'' — inside <code>data</code>, and again in the sibling <code>trackedItemID</code> field — and nothing checks that the two copies agree; a world whose copies disagree loads perfectly and silently never fires. Both take the item itself, or a raw id string for engine built-ins like <code>turn_number</code> and <code>player_action</code> that are not items in your world. Those two are listed in <code>iw.BUILTIN_TRACKED_ITEM_IDS</code>, which is what stops <code>validate()</code> rejecting a trigger that reads one; add to it if you meet another the engine supplies.

'''Every skill is a tracked item too.''' The engine makes one per entry in <code>skills</code>, named <code>skill_</code> plus the skill's own name lowercased with spaces underscored — a world with <code>skills=["Skill A", "Skill B"]</code> can read <code>skill_skill_a</code> and <code>skill_skill_b</code>. They never appear in <code>trackedItems</code>, so <code>validate()</code> derives them from <code>skills</code> rather than being told about them; a skill you rename renames its item.

== Notes ==

* Dataclasses use '''identity''' equality and hashing (<code>eq=False</code>), so instances are hashable and can be used as dict keys (which is how <code>plot</code> keys its stage maps). Two instances with identical fields are '''not''' equal — compare <code>.to_dict()</code> if you need value equality.
* Parsing is strict on purpose: an unknown field raises <code>NotImplementedError</code> rather than being dropped, so the dataclasses cannot quietly fall behind the engine's schema.
